headline: Qualified-certificate statements can be issued from a plain spec.
summary: The toolkit decoded eleven RFC 3739 qualified-certificate statement types and could build none of them, so issuing an EU qualified certificate meant hand-encoding every statementInfo. pki.x509.sign and pki.csr.sign now take qcStatements as a plain list, with a typed value for each statement the toolkit knows and pre-encoded DER for anything else.

Added: extensions.qcStatements takes a list of { statementId, info? } (RFC 3739 section 3.2.6). Each statement the toolkit knows encodes its own value syntax: qcCompliance and qcSSCD carry no info; qcType and qcIdentMethod take { types } or { methods } of object identifiers, including the registered ETSI names qctEsign, qctEseal and qctWeb; qcCClegislation and qcQSCDlegislation take { countries } of two-letter ISO 3166-1 codes; qcRetentionPeriod takes { years }; qcLimitValue takes { currency, amount, exponent } with an alphabetic three-letter or numeric 1 to 999 ISO 4217 currency; qcPDS takes { locations } of { url, language }; and qcsPkixQCSyntaxV1 and V2 take { semanticsIdentifier, nameRegistrationAuthorities }, at least one of the two. That is every statement type the parser reads back, so a certificate this builder emits decodes under the same syntax that reads it.

A statement id the toolkit does not know is reachable by supplying info as pre-encoded DER, and is refused if given a typed object, since nothing can infer the syntax of an unknown statement. The extension is emitted non-critical unless qcStatementsCritical is set: pki.path.validate does not process qcStatements, so a critical one is rejected as an unrecognized critical extension and pki.lint.certificate grades it lint/rfc5280/unknown-critical-extension.
qcStatements is accepted on the pki.csr.sign extensionRequest object as well, so a request and an issued certificate are written the same way.
